label: thm:A
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:A}
Let $T\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ be a triangle with vertices $(a,0,0)$, $(0,b,0)$, and $(0,0,c)$, for positive integers $a$, $b$, and $c$. Then the number of points in $T\cap\mathbb{Z}^3$ is given by the expression
\[
    \frac{\gcd(bc,ac,ab)}{2}+\frac{{\gcd(a,b)+\gcd(a,c)+\gcd(b,c)}}{2}+1.
\]
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: A method attributed to early Egyptians is to write the reciprocal of a positive integer $n$ as the sum of three unit fractions: $\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{n}$, for positive integers $a$, $b$, and $c$. Multiplying both sides of this equation by $abcn$ gives us $bcn+acn+abn=abc$. It follows that $\frac{1}{n}$ can be written as $\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}$ if and only if the point $(n,n,n)$ is on $T$.
head: environment

label: cor:B
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:B}
    Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive integers that all divide $n$. Then the number of solutions in nonnegative integers to $ax+by+cz=n$
    is given by the expression
    \[
        \frac{\gcd(n^2/bc,n^2/ac,n^2/ab)}{2}+\frac{\gcd(n/a,n/b)+\gcd(n/a,n/c)+\gcd(n/b,n/c)}{2}+1.
    \]
head: environment

label: example:1
title: Example
body_md:
\label{example:1}
    Let $B(n)$ denote the number of ways we can distribute $n$ objects among three bins without any requirement on how many objects must be grouped together to be placed in a bin. Clearly, $B(n)$ equals the number of solutions in nonnegative integers to $x+y+z=n$. Thus, by Corollary \ref{cor:B}, 
    \[
        B(n)=\frac{n^2}{2}+\frac{3n}{2}+1.
    \]

title: Definition
body_md:
Given a lattice $\Lambda\subset V$ with basis vectors $\vec{u}_1,\ldots,\vec{u}_d$, a {\it fundamental parallelepiped} of $\Lambda$ has the form
    \[
        \Pi=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^dx_i\vec{u}_i\;\left|\;0\le x_i\le1 \;\; {\rm for} \;\; i=1,\ldots,d\right.\right\}.
    \]
    The {\it determinant} of $\Lambda$, denoted $det(\Lambda)$, is defined to be the volume of $\Pi$, that is, $det(\Lambda)=Vol(\Pi)$.
head: environment

label: lem:simple is fundamental
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:simple is fundamental}
    Let $\Pi$ be a parallelepiped in $\Lambda$ that intersects $\Lambda$ only in the vertices of $\Pi$. Then $\Pi$ is a fundamental parallelepiped for $\Lambda$.
head: environment

title: Definition
head: environment
name: Special Triangle, Triangulation

title: Lemma
body_md:
Given a rank-2 integer lattice $\Lambda$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, let $T$ be a special triangle in $\Lambda$. Then 
    \[
        Area(T)=\frac{det(\Lambda)}{2}.
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that one of the vertices of $T$ is the origin. Let $\vec{u}$, $\vec{v}$, and $\vec{u}-\vec{v}$ denote sides of $T$ written as position vectors. We will show that the parallelogram $P$ determined by $\vec{u}-\vec{v}$ and $\vec{v}$ satisfies $|P\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|=4$ and is therefore a fundamental parallelogram for $\Lambda$ by Lemma \ref{lem:simple is fundamental}. Clearly $|\partial P\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|=4$. Thus we only need to show that $\overset{\circ}{P}\cap\mathbb{Z}^3=\emptyset$.
    
    Now, $\vec{u}$ is a diagonal of $P$ and divides $P$ into two congruent triangles, one of which is $T$. Let us call the other triangle $T'$. Suppose $T'$ contains the lattice vector $\vec{\lambda}$ in its interior. The transformation  $\vec{w}\mapsto\vec{u}-\vec{w}$ maps $T'$ bijectively onto $T$. The image of $\vec{\lambda}$, $\vec{u}-\vec{\lambda}$ is again in $\Lambda$. But $\vec{u}-\vec{\lambda}\in\overset{\circ}{T}$ by bijectivity, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:Picks in 3D
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Picks in 3D}
    Let $\Lambda$ be a rank 2 lattice in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Given a polygon $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with vertices in $\Lambda$, 
    \[
        |P\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|=\frac{Area(P)}{det(\Lambda)}+\frac{|\partial P\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|}{2}+1.
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we subdivide $P$ into special triangles, each having area $\frac{1}{2}det(\Lambda)$. Let $f$, $e$, and $v$ denote the numbers of faces, edges, and vertices, respectively, in $\Delta$. Then $f$ equals the number of special triangles in $P$. That is,
    \[
        f=2\frac{Area(P)}{det(\Lambda)}.
    \]
    Next, note that twice the number of special triangles in $P$ equals twice the number of edges in $\Delta$ minus the number of edges in $\partial P\cap\Delta$. In other words,
    \[
        6\frac{Area(P)}{det(\Lambda)}=2e-|\partial P\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|.
    \]
    Thus, the numbers of edges and vertices are
    \[
        e=3\frac{Area(P)}{det(\Lambda)}+\frac{|\partial P\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|}{2}  \hspace{1cm}\&\hspace {1cm}v=|P\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|,
    \]
    respectively. We can now apply Euler's Formula.
    \[
        1=f-e+v=2\frac{Area(P)}{det(\Lambda)}-3\frac{Area(P)}{det(\Lambda)}-\frac{|\partial P\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|}{2}+|P\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|
    \]
    Rearranging gives the desired result.

title: Definition
body_md: We call a triangle $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ {\it axial} if it has integral vertices with exactly one vertex contained on each axis.
head: environment

label: lem: fractional facts
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: fractional facts}
    Let $n,a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ where $b\nmid a$. Then
    \[
        \left\{n-\frac{a}{b}\right\}=1-\left\{\frac{a}{b}\right\}.
    \]
    For positive integers $i$ and $j$ with $i\equiv j\mod{\frac{b}{\gcd(a,b)}}$, we have
    \[
        \left\{\frac{ia}{b}\right\}=\left\{\frac{ja}{b}\right\}.
    \]
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Given a positive integer $n$ and a set of positive integers $A=\{a_1,\,a_2,\,\ldots,\,a_k\}$, we define the {\it restricted partition function} of $n$ with respect to $A$ by
    \[
        P_{A}(n)=\#\left\{(x_1,\,x_2,\,\ldots,\,x_k)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^k\;|\;a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_kx_k=n\right\}.
    \]

label: example:quasi polynomial
title: Example
body_md:
\label{example:quasi polynomial}
First, consider the unit square $S$ with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(1,1)$. Scaling $S$ by $t$ yields a square with vertices $(0,0)$, $(t,0)$, $(0,t)$, and $(t,t)$. We can apply Pick's Theorem (Equation \ref{eqn:Picks}) to enumerate the number of points on $tS$:
\[
    \mathcal{L}(t,S)=|tS\cap\mathbb{Z}^2|=t^2+\frac{4t}{2}+1.
\]
If we instead scale the rectangle $R$ with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,\frac{1}{2})$, and $(1,\frac{1}{2})$ by $t$, we find
\[
    \mathcal{L}(t,R)=\frac{1}{2}t^2+\left(\frac{3-t\;\text{mod}\,2}{2}\right)t+1-\frac{t\;\text{mod}\,2}{2},
\]
a quasi-polynomial with period 2.

label: thm:Clara1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Clara1}
    Given $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, 
    \[
        P_{\{bc,ac,ab\}}(abc)=\frac{\gcd(bc,ac,ab)}{2}+\frac{{\gcd(a,b)+\gcd(a,c)+\gcd(b,c)}}{2}+1.
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment
name: Proof 1.

title: Proof
body_md:
We perform the following transformations on $\mathbb{R}^3$. Shift by $-a$ along the $x$-axis, then reflect in the $yz$-plane. Given positive integers $a,b,c$, this has the effect of taking the plane $bcx+acy+abz=abc$ to the vector space $V$ with planar equation $bcx-acy-abz=0$. Let $\Lambda=V\cap\mathbb{Z}^3$. Since the transformations just described preserve the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^3\subset\mathbb{R}^3$, it follows that a special triangle on the plane $bcx+acy+abz=abc$ has area $det(\Lambda)/2$. 

    Now, $P_{\{bc,ac,ab\}}(abc)$ equals $|T\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|$, where $T$ is the triangle with vertices $(a,0,0)$, $(0,b,0)$, and $(0,0,c)$. If $T'$ denotes the image of $T$ under the transformations above then $|T\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|=|T'\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|$, $|\partial T\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|=|\partial T'\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|$, and $Area(T)=Area(T')$. Then, by Lemma \ref{lem:Picks in 3D},
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn:proof 2}
        |T\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|=\frac{Area(T)}{det(\Lambda)}+\frac{|\partial T\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|}{2}+1.
    \end{equation}
    By Equation \ref{eqn:det of Lambda}, 
    \[
        det(\Lambda)=\frac{\sqrt{(bc)^2+(ac)^2+(ab)^2}}{\gcd(bc,ac,ab)}.
    \]
    To get the area of $T$, we compute half the magnitude of
    \[
        \langle-a, b, 0\rangle\times\langle-a, 0, c\rangle=\langle bc,\; ac,\; ab\rangle.
    \]
    This gives
    \[
        Area(T)=\frac{\sqrt{(bc)^2+(ac)^2+(ab)^2}}{2}.
    \]
    Finally, note that the boundary of $T$ consists of three line segments, one in each coordinate plane. It follows that 
    \[
        |\partial T\cap\mathbb{Z}^3|=\gcd(a,b)+\gcd(a,c)+\gcd(b,c).
    \]
    The desired formula now follows after performing the necessary substitutions in Equation \ref{eqn:proof 2}.
head: environment
name: Proof 2.

label: cor:MainResult
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:MainResult}
    Given $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, let $l={\rm lcm}(a,b,c)$. For any nonnegative integer $k$,
    \[
        P_{\{a,b,c\}}(kl)=k^2\frac{\gcd(l^2/bc,l^2/ac,l^2/ab)}{2}+k\left(\frac{\gcd(l/a,l/b)+\gcd(l/a,l/c)+\gcd(l/b,l/c)}{2}\right)+1.
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A=k\frac{l}{a}$, $B=k\frac{l}{b}$, and $C=k\frac{l}{c}$. First note that $(x,y,z)$ is a solution to
    \[
        BCx+ACy+ABz=ABC
    \]
    if and only if it is a solution to $ax+by+cz=kl$. The desired expression then follows from computing
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{\gcd(BC,AC,AB)}{2}+\frac{{\gcd(A,B)+\gcd(A,C)+\gcd(B,C)}}{2}+1.
    \end{align*}
head: environment

label: rmk:Ehrhart Polynomials
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:Ehrhart Polynomials}
    We now describe the Ehrhart Polynomial corresponding to an axial triangle $T$ with vertices $(a,0,0)$, $(0,b,0)$, and $(0,0,c)$ by applying Theorem \ref{thm:Clara1} to the axial triangle with vertices $(ta,0,0)$, $(0,tb,0)$, and $(0,0,tc)$:
    \[
        \mathcal{L}(t,T)=P_{\{t^2bc,t^2ac,t^2ab\}}(t^3abc)= t^2\frac{\gcd(bc,ac,ab)}{2}+t\left(\frac{\gcd(a,b)+\gcd(a,c)+\gcd(b,c)}{2}\right)+1.
    \]
    We note however that Ehrhart's method for deriving such expressions was quite different. In a nutshell, Ehrhart equated the generating function $E(z)$ with expanding about the poles of certain rational expressions. Whereas our Proof 1 of Theorem \ref{thm:A} used mostly modular arithmetic.
head: environment

label: example:2
title: Example
body_md:
\label{example:2}
    Let $t\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ and $S$ denote the  axial triangle with vertices $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$, and $(0,0,1)$. As in Example \ref{example:1},
    \[
        \mathcal{L}(t,S)=\frac{t^2}{2}+\frac{3t}{2}+1.
    \]
    This equals $\binom{t+2}{2}$, the number of ways of choosing 2 objects from $t+2$ objects. By reciprocity,
    \[
        \mathcal{L}(t,\overset{\circ}{S})=\frac{t^2}{2}-\frac{3t}{2}+1=\binom{t-1}{2}.
    \]

label: eqn:upper bound 1
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ be pairwise relatively prime. Then
    \[
        P_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)=\sum_{i\ge0}P_{\{a,b\}}(n-ic).
    \]
    Since $\gcd(a,b)=1$, $P_{\{a,b\}}(n-ic)$ is nonzero for each $i=0,\ldots,\lfloor n/c\rfloor$. Thus,
    \[
        P_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}P_{\{a,b\}}(n-ic).
    \]
    Applying Lemma \ref{lem:P of a,b} yields
    \[
        P_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}\left(\frac{n-ic}{ab}-\left\{\frac{\beta(n-ic)}{a}\right\}-\left\{\frac{\alpha(n-ic)}{b}\right\}+1\right),
    \]
    where $\beta b\equiv1\mod a$ and $\alpha a\equiv1\mod b$. Many of the terms are easy to combine.
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}\left(\frac{n-ic}{ab}+1\right)=\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{c}\right\rfloor+1\right)\left(\frac{n+n\mod c}{2ab}+1\right).
    \end{equation*}
    Consider the sums
    \[
        \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}\left\{\frac{\beta(n-ic)}{a}\right\}\hspace{.5cm}\&\hspace{.5cm}\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}\left\{\frac{\alpha(n-ic)}{b}\right\}.
    \]
    We have
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}\left\{\frac{\beta(n-ic)}{a}\right\}=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}\left(\frac{\beta(n-ic)}{a}-\left\lfloor\frac{\beta(n-ic)}{a}\right\rfloor\right)
        =\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}\left(\frac{\beta(n-ic)\mod a}{a}\right).
    \end{equation*}
    Let $m=\lfloor n/c\rfloor$, and write $m=qa+r_a$, for $0\le r_a<a$ and $q>0$. Then
    \[
        \sum_{i=0}^m\beta(n-ic)\mod a=\sum_{i=0}^{aq-1}\beta(n-ic)\mod a+\sum_{i=aq}^{aq+r_a}\beta(n-ic)\mod a.
    \]
    Now,
    \[
        \sum_{i=0}^{aq-1}\beta(n-ic)\mod a=q\sum_{i=1}^{a-1}i=q\frac{a(a-1)}{2}=(\lfloor n/c\rfloor-\lfloor n/c\rfloor\mod a)\frac{a-1}{2}.
    \]
    Thus,
    \[
        \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}\left\{\frac{\beta(n-ic)}{a}\right\}=\frac{a-1}{2}\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}{a}\right\rfloor+\frac{1}{a}\sum_{i=0}^{r_a}\beta(n-ic)\mod a.
    \]
    Similarly, we can write $m=q'b+r_b$, for $0\le r_b<b$ and $q'>0$. Then
    \[
        \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}\left\{\frac{\alpha(n-ic)}{b}\right\}=\frac{b-1}{2}\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}{b}\right\rfloor+\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=0}^{r_b}\alpha(n-ic)\mod b.
    \]
    Now, the sum
    \[
        \sum_{i=0}^{r}\beta(n-ic)\mod a
    \]
    is always greater than or equal to 
    \[
        \sum_{i=0}^{r_a}i=\frac{r_a(r_a+1)}{2}
    \]
    and less than or equal to
    \[
        \sum_{i=0}^{r_a}a-1-i=(r_a+1)(a-1)-\frac{r_a(r_a+1)}{2}=(r_a+1)\frac{2a-r_a-2}{2}.
    \]
    Similarly,
    \[
        \frac{r_b(r_b+1)}{2}\le\sum_{i=0}^{r_b}\alpha(n-ic)\mod b\le(r_b+1)\frac{2b-r_b-2}{2}.
    \]
    For convenience in notation, given $a,b,c,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, we define
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn:upper bound 1}
        N_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)=\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{c}\right\rfloor+1\right)\left(\frac{n+n\mod c}{2ab}+1\right).
    \end{equation}
    An upper bound for $P_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)$ is then
    \[
        U_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)=N_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)-\left(\frac{a-1}{2}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{ac}\right\rfloor+\frac{r_a(r_a+1)}{2a}\right)-\left(\frac{b-1}{2}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{bc}\right\rfloor+\frac{r_b(r_b+1)}{2b}\right).
    \]
    And, a lower bound for $P_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)$ is given by
    \[
        L_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)=N_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)-\left(\frac{a-1}{2}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{ac}\right\rfloor+(r_a+1)\frac{2a-r_a-2}{2a}\right)-\left(\frac{b-1}{2}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{bc}\right\rfloor+(r_b+1)\frac{2b-r_b-2}{2b}\right).
    \]

    Now, let $Gap(n)=U_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)-L_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)$. Then
    \[
        Gap(n)=(r_a+1)\frac{a-r_a-1}{a}+(r_b+1)\frac{b-r_b-1}{b}.
    \]
    Letting $x=r_a+1$, the curve of $y=\frac{1}{a}x(a-x)$ is a parabola with a maximum value achieved when $x=a/2$. Similarly, the maximum value of $y=\frac{1}{b}x(b-x)$ is achieved when $x=b/2$. Thus,
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn:gap bound}
        Gap(n)\;\le\;(a/2)\frac{a-a/2}{a}+(b/2)\frac{b-b/2}{b}\;=\;\frac{a+b}{4}.
    \end{equation}

    Lastly, to show that $U_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)$ and $L_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)$ both have period $abc$, observe that $N_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)$ has period $c$, $\frac{a-1}{2}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{ac}\right\rfloor$ has period $ac$, $\frac{b-1}{2}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{bc}\right\rfloor$ has period $bc$, while $\frac{r_a(r_a+1)}{2a}$ and $(r_a+1)\frac{2a-r_a-2}{2a}$ both have period $a$, and $(r_b+1)\frac{2b-r_b-2}{2b}$ and $\frac{r_b(r_b+1)}{2b}$ both have period $b$. It follows that the periods of $U_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)$ and $L_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)$ are both ${\rm lcm}(a,b,c,ac,bc)={\rm lcm}(ac,bc)$. And, since $a$, $b$, and $c$ are pairwise relatively prime, lcm$(ac,bc)=c\,{\rm lcm}(a,b)=abc$.

title: Example
body_md:
Given $N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, the equation $5x+10y+25z=N$ has solutions if and only if $5|N$. Ignoring the cases with no solutions, we are able to simplify by dividing by $5$ yielding $x+2y+5z=n$, where $n=\frac{N}{5}$. Performing the necessary substitutions and simplifying, 
    $$U_{\{1,2,5\}}(n) = \left( \left\lfloor \frac{n}{5} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) \left( \frac{n + (n \bmod 5)}{4} + 1 \right) - \frac{1}{2}\left( \left\lfloor\frac{n}{10}\right\rfloor + \left\lfloor\frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor \bmod 2 \right)$$
    and
    $$L_{\{1,2,5\}}(n) = \left( \left\lfloor \frac{n}{5} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) \left( \frac{n + (n \bmod 5)}{4} + 1 \right) - \frac{1}{2}\left( \left\lfloor\frac{n}{10}\right\rfloor + 1 \right).$$
    In this case,
    $$\text{Gap}(n) = \frac{1 - \left(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor\bmod 2\right)}{2}.$$
    Thus, whenever $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor$ is odd, $U_{\{1,2,5\}}(n)$ and $L_{\{1,2,5\}}(n)$ both equal $P_{\{1,2,5\}}(n)$. When$\left\lfloor \frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor$ is even, $P_{\{1,2,5\}}(n)$ is given by whichever of $U_{\{1,2,5\}}(n)$ or $L_{\{1,2,5\}}(n)$ is an integer.

    More generally, when $a=1$ and $b=2$, we have $\text{Gap}(n)\le\frac{3}{4}$. In this case, $P_{\{1,2,c\}}(n)$ is easily obtained by calculating either $U_{\{1,2,c\}}(n)$ or $L_{\{1,2,c\}}(n)$ and then rounding appropriately.

body_md: Equation \ref{eqn:upper bound 1} yields another upper bound on $P_{\{a,b,c\}}(n)$. The bound is sharp when both $a$ and $b$ divide both $n$ and $c$.
